prose: Ars Technica reports that developer Brandon Thomas turned his Artcraft project, originally a controllable AI tool for artists, into seven open-source apps that copy the interface and tools of Adobe's Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign and Acrobat Pro.

He says he used Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 to write 'clean-room replacements' in Rust, with WebAssembly versions that run in a browser. The article's subtitle sums up the status: ambitious, free, and nowhere near finished. It sits within the argument over whether AI reverse engineering can make software cheap to copy, and how far 'clean-room' claims hold when a model does the work.
highlights: Artcraft pivots to seven open-source Adobe-style apps
Covers Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign and Acrobat
Built with Claude Opus 5.5 in Rust, plus WebAssembly builds
Ars calls them ambitious, free and far from finished
Raises questions about 'clean-room' claims with AI-assisted copying
